title: Product Strategy Write-Up: One-Page Strategy / PRD Outline
prompt: Write a one-page product strategy for the following goal: a mid-sized video-conferencing company wants to grow adoption among small businesses (under 50 employees), a segment where it currently lags a dominant competitor. Produce a concise strategy document / PRD outline: the problem and opportunity, target user and their needs, the strategy and why-now, what you'd build (scope and explicit non-goals), success metrics, key risks and tradeoffs, and a rough sequencing plan. Write it as you would for a leadership review.
blurb: A written product-strategy exercise — produce a crisp, leadership-ready one-pager with a clear thesis, prioritized scope, metrics, and risks.

rubric.label: Problem & opportunity framing
rubric.description: Frames the problem and the size/why of the opportunity crisply, grounded in the target segment's reality and the competitive gap — not vague ambition.

rubric.label: Target user & needs
rubric.description: Identifies the specific small-business user and their distinct needs and buying behavior (price sensitivity, no IT dept, ease/setup), distinguishing them from the enterprise buyer.

rubric.label: Strategy & 'why now'
rubric.description: Articulates a clear strategic thesis / wedge (how they'll win this segment against a dominant incumbent) and a credible why-now, not a feature list.

rubric.label: Scope, prioritization & non-goals
rubric.description: Defines a focused initial scope tied to the thesis AND explicit non-goals — demonstrating what they will deliberately NOT do.

rubric.label: Success metrics
rubric.description: Sets a north-star and supporting metrics (acquisition, activation, retention, monetization) with rough targets and guardrails.

rubric.label: Risks & tradeoffs
rubric.description: Names the main risks (competitive response, cannibalization, unit economics) and the tradeoffs the strategy accepts, with mitigations.

rubric.label: Structure & writing
rubric.description: Reads like a real one-pager: top-down thesis first, tight sections, scannable, concise, leadership-appropriate — no rambling or filler.

reference.scenario: Written deliverable, senior bar. The candidate submits a one-page strategy / PRD outline. There is no single correct strategy; strong submissions share: a sharp thesis for winning small businesses (SMB) against a dominant incumbent, a clear understanding that SMB buyers differ from enterprise (self-serve, price-sensitive, no IT, value setup speed and simplicity, often bottoms-up adoption), a focused wedge rather than 'match the competitor feature-for-feature', explicit non-goals, real metrics with targets, and honest risks. A common strong wedge: win on frictionless self-serve onboarding + SMB-tailored pricing/bundles + integrations with the tools small businesses already use, rather than competing on enterprise admin/security features that SMBs don't value. The interviewer evaluates the written artifact holistically against the rubric; it should be scannable and top-down.
model_points: Open with a one-line thesis / recommendation (top-down): how the company wins SMB and why it's worth doing now.

Problem & opportunity: the SMB segment is large and underpenetrated for this company; today the product and pricing are tuned for enterprise, so SMBs default to the incumbent. Quantify the opportunity roughly (segment size, current share, target share).

Target user & needs: the SMB decision-maker is often an owner/office-manager, not IT — they value fast self-serve setup, transparent affordable pricing, reliability, and integrations with existing tools; they do NOT value complex admin controls or procurement-heavy sales.

Strategy / wedge & why-now: pick a defensible angle (frictionless onboarding + SMB pricing/bundles + key integrations), and a why-now (remote/hybrid work normalizing video for small teams, incumbent complacent/expensive at the low end, a distribution or partnership opening).

Scope (what we build) AND explicit non-goals: e.g. build self-serve signup, a free/low tier, SMB-friendly billing, top 3 integrations, guided onboarding; NON-goals: enterprise SSO/admin console, custom procurement, telephony — deliberately deferred.

Success metrics: north-star (e.g. weekly active SMB paid teams, or activated teams retained at 30 days), plus acquisition (self-serve signups), activation (first successful hosted meeting), retention (M1/M3), monetization (free-to-paid conversion, ARPA), and guardrails (support cost/ticket rate, enterprise cannibalization).
Risks & tradeoffs with mitigations: competitive price response, low-tier unit economics / support cost, cannibalizing higher tiers, brand dilution — and how each is mitigated or monitored.
Sequencing: a rough phased plan (e.g. Phase 1 self-serve + pricing; Phase 2 integrations + onboarding polish; Phase 3 expansion/partnerships) with what unlocks the next phase.

probes.trigger: submission is a feature list with no thesis
probes.question: What is the one-sentence thesis for how you win this segment? Lead with it — why does this beat matching the incumbent feature-for-feature?
What are you deliberately NOT building or doing here? A strategy without non-goals isn't a strategy.

probes.trigger: treats SMB like a smaller enterprise
probes.question: How is the SMB buyer and their needs actually different from your enterprise buyer, and how does the plan reflect that?
What's your north-star metric and a rough target, and what guardrail keeps you from winning SMB at the expense of the core business?
Why is now the right time for this bet rather than a year ago or a year from now?
The dominant incumbent can cut prices or copy you. What's your risk here and how do you stay defensible?

red_flags: A feature list or wish list with no strategic thesis or wedge
No explicit non-goals / no evidence of prioritization
Treats SMB as a scaled-down enterprise; misunderstands the buyer
Vague or vanity metrics, no targets, no guardrails
Ignores competitive response, unit economics, or cannibalization
Rambling, not top-down, not scannable — reads like notes, not a leadership one-pager
Overreaches scope (tries to out-feature the incumbent everywhere) instead of a focused wedge
follow_ups: If leadership gives you only half the resources, what stays and what's cut from Phase 1?
How would you defend the low tier's unit economics if support costs balloon?
What would make you kill or pivot this strategy after two quarters — what's the disconfirming signal?
How do you prevent SMB pricing from cannibalizing your mid-market customers?
reference.exemplar_answer: A strong one-pager opens with a crisp thesis ('We win SMB by being the fastest, simplest, best-priced video tool for teams under 50 — not by out-featuring the incumbent'). Problem & opportunity: the SMB segment is large and underpenetrated; the product and pricing are enterprise-tuned, so SMBs default to the incumbent — with rough segment size, current share, and a target. Target user: an owner/office-manager, not IT, who values self-serve setup, transparent affordable pricing, reliability, and integrations with tools they already use, and is repelled by procurement and admin complexity. Strategy & why-now: a focused wedge — frictionless self-serve onboarding + SMB pricing/bundles + the top integrations — timed to hybrid-work normalization and an incumbent that's complacent and expensive at the low end. Scope names exactly what ships and, critically, explicit non-goals (enterprise SSO/admin, custom procurement, telephony — deferred). Metrics give a north-star (retained activated SMB paid teams) plus acquisition/activation/retention/monetization with rough targets and guardrails (support cost, cannibalization). Risks & tradeoffs are honest (price war, low-tier economics, cannibalization) each with a mitigation, and a phased sequencing plan shows what unlocks what. It's top-down, tight, and scannable — a document a VP could read in two minutes and act on.

interviewer_notes: This is a WRITTEN deliverable — evaluate the artifact, not a live dialogue. The senior bar is a genuine strategy: a sharp thesis/wedge, explicit non-goals, and prioritization, not a feature list. Reward top-down structure (thesis first), SMB-specific buyer insight, real metrics with targets and guardrails, and honest treatment of competitive response and unit economics. The most common senior-level miss is omitting non-goals and trying to out-feature the incumbent everywhere. If used interactively, deliver the probes as written feedback prompting a revision. Judge writing quality and scannability as part of the score — a leadership one-pager must be concise.
